title: Reflective practice & insight
blurb: What reflection and insight mean, the Gibbs, Kolb and Driscoll models, and how to write reflections that change your practice.
question: During a busy session you handed the dentist the wrong impression tray twice, and the patient had to wait. You felt flustered and embarrassed. How could you use a reflective model to turn this into learning, and what would show that you have insight?

teach.body: Reflective practice means reviewing an experience to understand what happened and work out what to do differently next time. Without reflection, you can repeat the same mistake for years. One of the nine duties of a dental nurse is to reflect on, review and develop the quality of your own practice. The GDC's Enhanced CPD scheme also expects your CPD record to show that you reflected on what you learned and how it changes your work.

Insight means understanding your own strengths, weaknesses and the effect your behaviour has on others. A nurse with insight says "I haven't done this before, can you show me?" instead of guessing. Insight also means noticing your own assumptions and biases about patients and colleagues. It matters for patient safety, because you ask for help before a mistake happens. It also matters when things go wrong: regulators look for whether a professional understands what happened and has learned from it.

teach.caption: Description: what happened? Feelings: what were you thinking and feeling? Evaluation: what was good and bad? Analysis: why did it happen? Conclusion: what else could you have done? Action plan: what will you do next time?

teach.body: Kolb's learning cycle has four stages: a concrete experience, reflective observation (looking back at it), abstract conceptualisation (forming new ideas) and active experimentation (trying them out). Driscoll's model uses three quick questions: What? So what? Now what? It's ideal for short, everyday reflections. Schön separated reflection-in-action, thinking on your feet while something is happening, from reflection-on-action, looking back afterwards.

teach.caption: The GDC doesn't prescribe a model. Use whichever helps you learn, on your own or with a mentor or peer.

teach.body: A good reflection is honest and focused on learning, not just a description of events. Ask what you learned, why it matters for patients and what you will change. Keep written reflections free of anything that could identify a patient, such as names, addresses or dates of birth. After a CPD activity, note how it will change your practice and whether your PDP needs adjusting. Record in your CPD log that reflection has taken place.

rows.label: Example
values: "I learned our foil test was overdue, so I've booked it"

teach.text: Reflection is not a diary or a list of courses. The exam test is always: what did you learn, and what will you do differently?

items: Reflective practice: reviewing an experience to identify what to do differently.
Reflection shows how learning will change your practice; the GDC expects it in your CPD record.
Insight: knowing your limits, biases and impact, and asking for help early.
Gibbs: Description, Feelings, Evaluation, Analysis, Conclusion, Action plan.
Kolb: experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation. Driscoll: What? So what? Now what?
Keep reflections anonymous: no patient-identifiable details.

summary: You can now define reflective practice and insight, work through Gibbs' six stages, recognise Kolb's cycle, Driscoll's three questions and Schön's in-action and on-action reflection, and write an anonymised reflection that shows how your practice will change.

A.q: Which description of reflective practice is most accurate?
options: Writing down everything that happened in detail
Reviewing an experience to decide what to change
Listing every CPD course completed during the year
A.why: Reflective practice means reviewing an experience to understand it and identify what to do differently.

whyNot.0: Description alone is only the first step; reflection goes on to learning and change.
whyNot.2: A list of courses is a log, not reflection.
whyNot.3: Discussing others' mistakes informally isn't structured self-reflection.

A.q: In Gibbs' reflective cycle, which stage comes straight after 'Feelings'?
A.why: The order is Description, Feelings, Evaluation, Analysis, Conclusion, Action plan.

whyNot.0: Description is the first stage, before Feelings.
whyNot.1: Action plan is the final stage.
whyNot.2: Conclusion comes after Evaluation and Analysis.

A.q: A dental nurse realises she is unsure how to use a new sterilizer and asks for training before running it. What does this show?
options: Poor time management on a busy day
A failure to follow practice policy
Reluctance to take on new work
A.why: Recognising the limits of your knowledge and asking for help is insight, and it protects patients.

whyNot.0: Taking time to be trained is safe practice, not poor time management.
whyNot.2: Asking for training is exactly what policy expects.
whyNot.3: She is preparing to do the task safely, not avoiding it.

B.q: What does reflection add to a CPD activity?
options: It shows how learning will change practice
It doubles the number of verifiable hours you claim
It replaces the need for a certificate
It proves the course was quality assured
B.why: Reflection identifies what you learned and how it will change your daily practice.

whyNot.1: Reflection doesn't change the hours on your certificate.
whyNot.2: Verifiable CPD still needs provider evidence.
whyNot.3: Quality assurance comes from the provider, not your reflection.

B.q: Which reflective model is built around three questions: 'What? So what? Now what?'
B.why: Driscoll's model uses these three questions and is quick to use for everyday reflection.

whyNot.3: Schön described reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action, not three questions.

B.q: A nurse writes in her reflective log: "Mary Smith of 14 High Street fainted during treatment." What is wrong with this entry?
options: It is too short to count as reflection
It should be written by the dentist
B.why: Written reflections should be anonymised, with no names or details that could identify the patient.

whyNot.0: Length isn't the problem here; confidentiality is.
whyNot.1: Every registrant writes their own reflections.
whyNot.2: Medical emergencies are valuable events to reflect on.

C.q: Which stage of Gibbs' cycle asks 'What will I do if this happens again?'
C.why: The Action plan stage sets out what you will do differently next time.

whyNot.1: Evaluation asks what was good and bad about the experience.

C.q: During a procedure, a nurse notices the suction isn't clearing fluid well and repositions the tip straight away. Which type of reflection is this?
C.why: Reflection-in-action is thinking on your feet and adjusting while the event is happening.

whyNot.2: Peer review involves colleagues reviewing practice, not an instant adjustment.
whyNot.3: Significant event analysis is a team review after an event.

C.q: Why is insight important for a dental nurse?
options: It lets you work beyond your scope safely
It means you no longer need supervision
It helps you recognise limits and seek help
It replaces the need to do any CPD
C.why: Insight helps you recognise your limits, ask for help early and keep patients safe.

whyNot.0: Nothing allows you to work beyond your scope.
whyNot.1: Insight includes knowing when you still need supervision.
whyNot.3: Insight often shows you what CPD you need.

reteach.title: What? So what? Now what?
reteach.question: Forget the six-stage cycle for a moment. If you only had three questions to reflect on the wrong-tray mix-up, what would they be?

blocks.body: A footballer watches a replay of a missed chance. First: what actually happened? Next: so what, why did it go wrong and does it matter? Last: now what, what will I practise before the next match? That's reflection. Any model, short or long, follows the same path from what happened, to why it matters, to what you'll change.

steps.label: What?
steps.sub: I handed the wrong tray twice

steps.label: So what?
steps.sub: Patient waited; I hadn't checked the plan

steps.label: Now what?
steps.sub: Check every plan before the session starts

blocks.text: If your reflection has no 'Now what?', it is only a description.

explain.body: Six stages in order: Description, Feelings, Evaluation, Analysis, Conclusion, Action plan. It suits a detailed reflection on a single event.

steps.label: Feelings
steps.sub: What did I think and feel?

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.sub: What else could I have done?

steps.label: Action plan
steps.sub: What will I do next time?

test.q: What is the FIRST stage of Gibbs' reflective cycle?
test.why: Gibbs' cycle starts with Description: what happened?

whyNot.3: Action plan is the sixth and final stage.

explain.body: Concrete experience, then reflective observation, then abstract conceptualisation (forming new ideas), then active experimentation (trying them out), which creates a new experience.

test.q: In Kolb's cycle, what follows abstract conceptualisation (forming new ideas)?
test.why: After forming new ideas, you test them out in practice: active experimentation.

whyNot.0: Concrete experience starts the cycle and follows experimentation.
whyNot.1: Reflective observation comes before forming new ideas.
whyNot.3: Description is a stage of Gibbs' cycle, not Kolb's.

explain.body: Driscoll: What? So what? Now what? Schön: reflection-in-action happens during the event; reflection-on-action happens afterwards.

test.q: That evening, a nurse thinks back over a difficult appointment and decides what to change next time. Which type of reflection is this?
test.why: Looking back on an event afterwards is reflection-on-action.

whyNot.1: Audit measures practice against a standard.
whyNot.2: Appraisal is a meeting with your manager.

explain.body: Insight means knowing your limits, biases and the effect you have on others, and acting on that knowledge, for example by asking for help before you guess.

options: Hiding a mistake to avoid embarrassment
"I've not done this; can you show me first?"
Blaming the equipment for every error you make
test.why: Recognising a gap in your skills and asking for help shows insight.

whyNot.0: Hiding mistakes shows a lack of insight and risks patient safety.
whyNot.2: Assuming you're always right shows a lack of insight.
